question.worked_solution:
To subtract $-\frac{3}{2}$ from $1$, we drop  the parentheses and combine the two negative signs to make a single plus sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-(-\frac{3}{2})=1+\frac{3}{2} & .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the two numbers as fractions over a common denominator of $2$
 and combine the numerators. This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{2}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=\frac{2+3}{2} & .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we work out $2+3$ using our number line.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14150464/assets/c83beb4c78b8690dc04d2cc95bb20e94e33eac19962edea1055089adb4213ad4.png)

So we get

$$
\frac{2+3}{2}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$
